course.title: Sealed Types and Patterns
course.description: Most domain bugs are not wrong arithmetic. They are a case nobody handled: the refund path for an order that was paid but not shipped, the payment method added last quarter that one report forgot. Sealed types make the set of cases a fact the compiler and the runtime both know. Records make each case plain data, and patterns take a value apart safely. Together they are the Java version of what functional languages call algebraic data types, and they change how you model a domain: instead of one class with nullable fields and a `type` string, you get one small record per case and code that cannot confuse them.

lessons.title: Sealed Types and Patterns
lessons.explanation:
# 15 · Sealed Types and Patterns

Most domain bugs are not wrong arithmetic. They are a case nobody
handled: the refund path for an order that was paid but not shipped,
the payment method added last quarter that one report forgot. Sealed
types make the set of cases a fact the compiler and the runtime both
know. Records make each case plain data, and patterns take a value
apart safely. Together they are the Java version of what functional
languages call algebraic data types, and they change how you model a
domain: instead of one class with nullable fields and a `type` string,
you get one small record per case and code that cannot confuse them.

This module is written for **Java 17**: sealed types, records and
`instanceof` patterns are final there. Pattern `switch` and record
patterns arrived in Java 21. Each section shows what 17 gives you and
what 21 adds, so you can read both kinds of codebase.

## The mental model

### 1 · Sealed = a closed list of cases

```java
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rect, Triangle {}
record Circle(double radius) implements Shape {}
record Rect(double width, double height) implements Shape {}
```

Only the listed types may implement `Shape`. A permitted subtype must
be `final` (records are), `sealed` itself, or `non-sealed` (open again,
on purpose). The list can be read at runtime:
`Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses()`.

### 2 · Patterns: test, cast and bind in one step

```java
if (s instanceof Rect r && r.width() == r.height()) return "square";
if (!(v instanceof String text)) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
return text.strip();                       // flow scoping: text is bound here
```

Java 17 has `instanceof` patterns with `&&` guards. Java 21 adds:

```java
return switch (s) {                        // Java 21: checked for exhaustiveness
    case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();
    case Rect(double w, double h) -> w * h; // a record pattern
    case Triangle t -> heron(t);
};                                         // no default: a missing case does not compile
```

In 17 an `instanceof` chain ends with `throw new AssertionError(...)`,
because the compiler cannot prove the chain is complete.

### 3 · Two ways to add an operation: visitor or sealed dispatch

| | adding an operation | adding a case | where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| visitor (`accept` + `Visitor<R>`) | new class, no node changes | every visitor changes | javac tree API, ASM, ANTLR |
| sealed + patterns | new static method | every method changes; Java 21 tells you where | modern domain code |
| plain subclass methods | every class changes | one new class | classic OO |

This trade-off is the "expression problem". Sealed types choose "cases
are fixed, operations grow", which suits domains like payments, order
states and JSON, where the cases rarely change and new reports and
rules arrive every sprint.

### 4 · Errors and states as values

```
Result<T>  = Ok(value) | Err(message)                    parse, validate, import
OrderState = Draft(items) | Paid(items, paymentId) | Shipped(..., tracking) | ...
Json       = JNull | JBool | JNum | JStr | JArr | JObj
```

Each case carries exactly the data that exists in that case. A
`Shipped` has a tracking number; a `Draft` cannot have one, so no code
can read one by mistake. Transitions are pure functions
`(state, event) -> state`, which is what makes replay and testing easy.

## The details that bite

1. **Validate with `!(x > 0)`, not `x <= 0`.** NaN fails every
   comparison, so `<=` lets it in (exercise 01).
2. **"Sides must close" is strict.** 1, 2, 3 is a flat line
   (exercise 01).
3. **Order the checks: specific before general.** A blank-text check
   after the any-text check never runs (exercise 02).
4. **Narrow only after a range check.** `(int) 3_000_000_000L` is
   negative; `Integer.parseInt("99999999999")` throws (exercise 02).
5. **Use `Math.addExact` and friends.** Plain `+` wraps silently
   (exercise 03).
6. **Rewrite bottom-up.** Simplify the children first, or `x + 2*0`
   stays unsimplified (exercise 03).
7. **`map` on an `Err` must not call `f`, and `sequence` returns the
   FIRST error** (exercise 04).
8. **`"AB,".split(",")` drops the empty field.** Use `split(",", -1)`
   (exercise 04).
9. **Pre-order versus post-order.** Collect a link before the links
   nested inside it (exercise 05).
10. **Escape your own syntax characters** in Markdown and in JSON
    strings (exercises 05, 07).
11. **Refuse every transition you did not list.** A silently accepted
    "cancel after ship" is a lost parcel (exercise 06).
12. **Whole doubles print as `3.0`.** Print them as longs, but only
    within the exact range (exercise 07).
13. **Merge patch recurses into objects;** replacing the whole object
    loses its other fields (exercise 07).
14. **The nearest handler wins.** A leaf's own handler beats its sealed
    parent's, which beats the root's (exercise 08).

## Cheat table

| want | Java 17 | Java 21 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| closed set of cases | `sealed interface X permits A, B` | same |
| case with data | `record A(int n) implements X` | same |
| test and bind | `x instanceof A a` | same, plus `case A a ->` |
| guard | `x instanceof A a && a.n() > 0` | `case A a when a.n() > 0 ->` |
| destructure | `a.n()` accessors | `case A(int n) ->` |
| exhaustiveness | runtime check via `getPermittedSubclasses()` | the compiler, in `switch` |
| one-off singleton case | `enum JNull implements Json { INSTANCE }` | same |

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-sealed-shapes.java` | ★☆☆ | sealed records with validation, area, a guarded `describe` |
| 02 | `02-instanceof-patterns.java` | ★☆☆ | safe narrowing and classification of untyped config values |
| 03 | `03-expression-evaluator.java` | ★★☆ | eval, show and simplify over an expression tree |
| 04 | `04-result-type.java` | ★★☆ | a sealed `Result<T>` with map/flatMap, and an order-line parser |
| 05 | `05-visitor-vs-sealed.java` | ★★☆ | the same document operations as visitors and as sealed dispatch |
| 06 | `06-sealed-state-machine.java` | ★★☆ | an order lifecycle where each state carries its own data |
| 07 | `07-json-adt.java` | ★★★ | a JSON value type: render, path lookup, merge patch |
| 08 | `08-exhaustive-dispatch.java` | ★★★ | a dispatcher that refuses to build with an unhandled case |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows. Exercise 06
is module 08's state machine with types instead of an enum, and its
`replay` is the event-sourcing fold from module 12. Exercise 04's
`Result` is built the same way as 14's pipeline. The next module uses
these types inside design patterns.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/16-design-patterns`

unit.title: A state machine of sealed states

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** sealed interfaces · records · instanceof patterns · guards  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A floor-plan tool knows exactly three shapes: Shape is sealed and
permits Circle, Rect and Triangle, each a record. Finish:

  the compact constructors   every size must be > 0 (NaN is rejected
                             too), and a Triangle's sides must close:
                             each side SHORTER than the other two
                             together; else IllegalArgumentException
  area(s), perimeter(s)      triangle area by Heron's formula
  describe(s)                "circle r=2.0", "square 3.0" for a Rect
                             with equal sides, "rect 2.0x3.0",
                             "triangle 3.0/4.0/5.0"
  permittedNames()           Shape's permitted subclasses' simple
                             names, sorted, read at runtime

    area(new Rect(2, 3))      → 6.0
    describe(new Rect(3, 3))  → "square 3.0"

hint: `s instanceof Rect r && r.width() == r.height()` is one test.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
A SEALED interface lists every implementation up front (permits ...),
so the set of shapes is closed: nobody can add a Hexagon behind your
back, and code that handles all three really handles all of them.
Records are the natural partner: each case is plain data with
equals, hashCode and toString for free, plus a compact constructor
for its invariants.
Java 17 dispatches with instanceof patterns: `if (s instanceof Circle
c) return Math.PI * c.radius() * c.radius();`. The binding c exists
only where the test is true, and `&&` can extend it into a guard, as
describe does for squares. The chain ends with `throw new
AssertionError(...)`: Java 17 cannot prove an if-chain exhaustive. Java
21's `switch (s) { case Circle c -> ... }` can, and then the compiler
flags a missing case when a shape is added.
Validate with !(radius > 0), not radius <= 0: every comparison with
NaN is false, so "<= 0" lets NaN through. The triangle check must be
strict: sides 1, 2, 3 lie flat and enclose no area.
getPermittedSubclasses() (Java 17) reads the permits list by
reflection, which the last exercise of this module builds on.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** instanceof patterns · guards · flow scoping · check order  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A config loader hands you plain Objects. Finish three helpers:

  asInt(v)   Integer → itself; Long → only if it fits an int; Double →
             only if whole and within int range; String → stripped
             text of an optional "-" and digits, if it fits an int;
             anything else (null, Boolean, lists...) → empty
  kind(v)    "null"; "integer" for Integer/Long/Short/Byte; "decimal"
             for Double/Float/BigDecimal; "blank text" for a blank
             CharSequence; "text" for any other CharSequence;
             "collection of N" / "map of N" with the size; otherwise
             "other: " + the class's simple name
  requireText(v, field)  v as stripped text; if v is not a String or
             is blank, IllegalArgumentException "<field> must be text"

    asInt(3_000_000_000L)  → empty       asInt(" -12 ") → -12
    kind("  ")             → "blank text"

hint: `if (!(v instanceof String s)) throw ...;` keeps s in scope below.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
An instanceof PATTERN tests and binds in one step: `v instanceof Long
l` gives you l as a Long, no cast. A pattern can carry a GUARD with &&
(`v instanceof CharSequence cs && cs.toString().isBlank()`), and the
order of the checks is part of the logic: test the special case
(blank) before the general one (any CharSequence), exactly like the
order of catch blocks.
FLOW SCOPING is the less known half. After `if (!(v instanceof String
s)) throw ...;` the compiler knows that s is definitely bound on the
lines below, so requireText reads like straight-line code.
Narrowing is where the bugs live. (int) 3_000_000_000L silently wraps
to a negative number, so check the range first. A Double is whole when
d == Math.rint(d); NaN fails that test (NaN equals nothing) and
infinities fail the range check. Parsing a String with
Integer.parseInt throws on "99999999999"; matching the shape first,
then parsing as a long and range-checking, turns every bad input into
an empty Optional rather than an exception.
In Java 21 `switch (v) { case Long l when ... -> }` does the same with
the same rule: specific cases first.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** algebraic data types · recursion · exact arithmetic · rewriting  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A pricing-formula engine stores formulas as a sealed tree: Num, Var,
Add, Mul and Neg records. Finish four recursive functions:

  eval(e, env)   the long value; an unknown Var throws
                 NoSuchElementException naming it; overflow throws
                 ArithmeticException
  show(e)        infix text: "a + b", "a * b", "-x"; an Add operand of a
                 Mul gets parentheses; a Neg operand that is not a Num
                 or Var gets parentheses; nothing else does
  simplify(e)    children first, then: Num op Num folds to a Num;
                 x + 0 and 0 + x → x; x * 1 and 1 * x → x; x * 0 and
                 0 * x → 0; -(Num n) → Num(-n); -(-x) → x
  variables(e)   each Var name once, sorted

    show(Mul(Add(a, 1), b))                 → "(a + 1) * b"
    simplify(Add(Var x, Mul(Num 2, Num 0))) → Var x

hint: Math.addExact and friends throw on overflow so you do not have to.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
This is the classic algebraic data type: a sealed interface with one
record per case, and functions that recurse over the tree. Each
function is an instanceof chain with one branch per case, so adding a
new operation (show, simplify, variables...) touches no existing
class. Adding a new CASE touches every function: that is the
expression problem, and the visitor exercise next looks at the other
side of it.
eval uses Math.addExact, multiplyExact and negateExact, which throw
ArithmeticException on overflow. Plain + wraps silently to a negative
price, the worst kind of bug in a pricing engine.
show puts parentheses only where precedence needs them: a sum inside a
product, and a compound operand of a negation. Parenthesising
everything is correct but unreadable; never parenthesising is wrong.
simplify must work BOTTOM-UP: simplify the children, then look at the
node. Top-down misses rewrites that only appear after a child has been
simplified: x + (2 * 0) only becomes x + 0, and then x, if the product
is folded first. Records make the rebuilt tree cheap to compare in
the tests: two trees are equal when their components are.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** sealed generics · Result/Either · map/flatMap · error values  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An order import reports bad lines as values, not exceptions. Result<T>
is sealed: Ok(value) or Err(error message). Finish:

  map(f), flatMap(f)  f applied to an Ok; an Err passes through, f unused
  mapError(f)         rewrite an Err's message; an Ok passes through
  orElse(fallback)    the Ok's value, or the fallback for an Err
  attempt(work)       Ok of work's result; if it throws, Err of the
                      message, or of the exception's simple class name
                      when the message is null
  sequence(results)   Ok of all values in order, or the FIRST Err
  parseLine(line)     "sku,qty", spaces around either part allowed; else
                      Err "expected sku,qty: <line>" (not 2 parts),
                      "missing sku", "bad quantity: <q>" (not an int)
                      or "quantity must be positive: <q>"
  parseOrder(lines)   Ok of all lines, or the first Err as "line N: ..."

    parseOrder(["A,1", "B,x"])  → Err("line 2: bad quantity: x")
hint: split(",", -1) keeps trailing empty parts; split(",") drops them.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
Exceptions are for the unexpected; a bad line in an import file is
expected, and the caller wants to collect or report it. A Result type
makes the failure part of the return type, so it cannot be ignored by
accident. Java has no built-in one; Rust's Result, Scala's Either and
Vavr's Try are the same idea.
Result<T> is sealed with two record cases, and its operations are
default methods that dispatch with `this instanceof Ok<T> ok`. Java 17
allows the generic pattern because the check from Result<T> to Ok<T>
is safe. map and flatMap leave an Err untouched and never call f: that
short-circuit is what lets a chain of steps stop at the first failure
without any if-statements.
sequence turns a List<Result<T>> into a Result<List<T>>, returning on
the first Err. Keeping the last error instead reports the wrong line.
The parse trap: "AB,".split(",") gives ["AB"], one part, so the error
would be the wrong one; split(",", -1) keeps the empty quantity and
reports "bad quantity: ". The line number is added with mapError per
line, before sequencing, so the message knows which line it came from.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** visitor pattern · double dispatch · sealed dispatch · trees  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A help-centre article is a tree: Text, Bold(children) and Link(url,
children). Each node already has accept(Visitor). Write the operations
two ways. As Visitors:

  PlainText       all text, formatting dropped
  Markdown        Bold → **inner**, Link → [inner](url); in Text, put a
                  backslash before each * [ and ]
  LinkCollector   every url in document order (a link before the links
                  nested inside it)
  NodeCounter     the number of nodes, containers included
As sealed dispatch with instanceof:
  depth(n)        Text is 1; a container is 1 + its deepest child (1
                  when it has no children)
  mapText(n, f)   the same tree with f applied to every Text

    Markdown: Bold[Text "hi ", Link(u, [Text "x"])] → **hi [x](u)**

hint: a visitor method can call accept on children with `this`.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
The VISITOR pattern (Gang of Four) gives a closed set of node types an
open set of operations without instanceof: each node's accept calls
the one visitX method for its own type ("double dispatch"), and each
operation is a class implementing Visitor<R>. Adding NodeCounter
touched no node class. The cost: adding a node type (Image, say) means
a new visitImage on the interface and in every visitor.
A sealed hierarchy with instanceof (and Java 21's pattern switch) gets
the same open set of operations with less ceremony: depth and mapText
are plain static methods. Visitors still earn their keep when the
operations are many and stateful, when the hierarchy predates sealed
types (javac's own tree API, ASM, ANTLR), or when a library wants
callers to plug in operations without seeing the internals.
The details: LinkCollector adds the url BEFORE visiting children
(pre-order), so the outer link comes first. Markdown must escape the
characters it uses as syntax, or a price like "2*3" turns bold.
mapText rebuilds containers around the mapped children and keeps
the url; records make "same structure" a single equals check.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** sealed states · records carry state data · transitions  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

Sealed order states hold only the data each state has: Draft(items),
Placed(items), Paid(items, paymentId), Shipped(items, paymentId,
tracking), Cancelled(reason, refundDue). apply(state, event) gives:

  Draft + AddItem(sku) → Draft with sku appended
  Draft + Place → Placed (no items: "cannot place an empty order")
  Placed + Pay(id) → Paid;  Paid + Ship(t) → Shipped
  Draft or Placed + Cancel(r) → Cancelled(r, false)
  Paid + Cancel(r) → Cancelled(r, true)
Refusals are IllegalStateExceptions; any other pair gives "cannot
<Event> when <State>" in simple class names: "cannot Ship when Placed".
replay(events) applies each from an empty Draft. allowedEvents(state)
names the events apply accepts, in the order AddItem, Place, Pay,
Ship, Cancel (Draft lists Place even when empty).

    replay([AddItem a, Place, Pay p1]) → Paid([a], p1)

hint: check the pair (state, event); one instanceof per side.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
An enum state machine (module 08) knows WHICH state an order is in. A
sealed hierarchy of records also knows what the order HAS in that
state: only Paid and Shipped carry a paymentId, only Shipped a
tracking number, only Cancelled a refund flag. An "order" class with
nullable fields for all of them lets code read a tracking number that
cannot exist yet; here the type system rules it out.
apply is a pure function (state, event) -> state. It never mutates:
Draft's compact constructor copies the list, and AddItem builds a new
list. Pure transitions are what make replay (event sourcing, module
12) and testing trivial: the same events always give the same state.
Every pair not listed is refused with one uniform message. The trap
is a transition that "works" silently: a cancel after shipping that
returns Cancelled would lose the parcel. Paid + Cancel is the one
place that sets refundDue: the payment has to be reversed.
allowedEvents is derived from apply itself, by trying each event, so
the UI's buttons can never disagree with the rules. Java 21 would let
you write apply as one switch over a record pattern of the pair.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** algebraic data types · enum singleton · escaping · merge patch  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

JSON as a sealed type: JNull (an enum singleton), JBool, JNum, JStr,
JArr and JObj (fields keep insertion order). Finish:

  JNum(v)     NaN or an infinity → IllegalArgumentException
  render(j)   compact JSON. A whole number below 1e15 in size prints as
              a long ("3"; -0.0 as "0"), others by Double.toString
              ("1.0E20"). In strings escape " and \ with a backslash,
              newline as \n, tab as \t, other chars below 0x20 as a
              backslash, "u" and 4 lowercase hex digits ("u0001")
  at(j, path) follow a dot path ("orders.1.sku"): a field name in a
              JObj, a 0-based index in a JArr; else empty; "" → the root
  merge(base, patch)  JSON Merge Patch: a non-object patch replaces
              base; an object patch applies field by field, recursing;
              a JNull value removes the field; new fields go last

    merge({"a":1,"b":2}, {"b":3,"a":null,"c":4})  → {"b":3,"c":4}

hint: the recursion in merge is on the field's old value and new value.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
JSON is a textbook sum type: a value is exactly one of six cases, so a
sealed interface of five records and one enum models it with nothing
left over. JNull is an enum constant because there is only one null;
an enum can implement a sealed interface like any class can.
render is a recursive walk with one branch per case. The bugs are in
the leaves. Double.toString(3.0) is "3.0", which some consumers parse
as a float, so whole numbers print as longs (only below 1e15, where a
double still holds every integer exactly). Strings need escaping of
the quote, the backslash and every control character, or the output
is not JSON. This is why you never build JSON by concatenation.
at returns Optional because a path is data from outside: a missing
field, a bad index and the wrong container type are all "not there",
not exceptions. Check the index bound before get, or an
IndexOutOfBoundsException escapes.
merge is RFC 7386, the format of HTTP PATCH with
application/merge-patch+json. Recursing into nested objects is the
point: patching {"user":{"city":"Lima"}} must keep the user's name.
A LinkedHashMap copy of the base keeps field order stable.

javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.instructions:
**Concepts:** exhaustiveness · getPermittedSubclasses · isSealed · registries  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

Java 17 cannot check that an instanceof chain covers every case. Build
a Dispatcher that checks it when it is built, from the permits lists.
Payments: Card, BankTransfer and Wallet, where Wallet is itself sealed
(ApplePay, PayPal). A permitted type that is not sealed is a LEAF.

  leaves(root)       simple names of every leaf under root, sorted
  forSealed(root)    a Builder; a root that is not sealed throws
                     IllegalArgumentException
  on(type, handler)  register; the same type twice → IllegalStateException
  build()            each leaf is covered by its own handler or, if it
                     has none, by the NEAREST registered ancestor
                     (Wallet, or the root itself); uncovered leaves →
                     IllegalStateException "unhandled: A, B" (sorted)
  dispatch(value)    run the handler that covers value's class

    on(Card) on(Wallet) on(BankTransfer) → build OK; PayPal → Wallet's

hint: Class has isSealed() and getPermittedSubclasses() since Java 17.
javabootcamp/15-sealed-types-and-pattern.explanation:
With an enum, a switch expression is checked: leave out a constant and
javac refuses. With sealed types in Java 17 there is no such check
yet: an instanceof chain that forgets a case compiles, and the bug
shows up as the AssertionError at its end. Java 21's pattern switch
closes the gap at compile time. This exercise closes it at startup:
the permits lists are readable by reflection, so build() can walk the
hierarchy and refuse to create a dispatcher with a hole in it. Failing
when the application starts, with the missing names, is the next best
thing to failing at compile time, and it is how frameworks validate
handler registries and serializers.
The walk is recursive: a sealed type's permitted subclasses are leaves
or more sealed types, and the handler for a leaf is its own, or the
nearest one inherited on the way down. Resolving every leaf once in
build() makes dispatch a single map lookup on value.getClass().
The registry stores Function<Object, R> wrappers that type.cast(...)
the value. The generic on(Class<S>, Function<? super S, ...>) has
already guaranteed the cast cannot fail, and a raw call will fail at
the cast instead of deep inside a handler.
